THE CORE IDEA

runs.text: Disinflation lowers the inflation rate but usually creates temporary output and employment costs while expectations adjust. Contraction reduces aggregate demand and inflation pressure, normally creating a short-run output gap and higher unemployment. Expected inflation adjusts, the SRPC shifts, and unemployment returns toward its natural rate. Disinflation is a decline in the inflation rate; deflation is a decline in the price level.

WORKED EXAMPLE: LOWERING INFLATION

runs.text: Horizontal axis: unemployment rate; vertical axis: inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower, leftward downward-sloping curve; SRPC2 is the higher, rightward downward-sloping curve. Point a on SRPC1 is at unemployment U1 and inflation I2. Point b, where SRPC2 meets LRPC, is at U2 and I2. Point c, where SRPC1 meets LRPC, is at U2 and I1. Point d on SRPC2 is at U3 and I1. From left to right the unemployment labels are U1, U2, U3; I2 is above I1. Dashed guides identify all four points. No numerical rates are printed.

Point b, where SRPC2 meets LRPC, is at U2 and I2. Point c, where SRPC1 meets LRPC, is at U2 and I1. Point d on SRPC2 is at U3 and I1. From left to right the unemployment labels are U1, U2, U3; I2 is above I1. Dashed guides identify all four points. No numerical rates are printed.

runs.text: Contractionary policy first moves the economy along SRPC2 from b to d, lowering inflation from I2 to I1 while unemployment rises from U2 to U3. As expected inflation adjusts downward, SRPC shifts to SRPC1 and unemployment returns to U2 at point c. Disinflation creates a temporary employment cost.
